title: Training an MoE LLM in MXFP4: How We Closed the Gap to BF16

Title:Training an MoE LLM in MXFP4: How We Closed the Gap to BF16
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Training large language models (LLMs) in sub-8-bit arithmetic promises substantial gains in memory bandwidth and compute throughput, yet FP4 formats introduce quantization error severe enough to destabilize optimization if left unaddressed. We present ALTO, an open-source training recipe for GPT-OSS-20B, a 20-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts (MoE) model, on the MLPerf Small MoE Training benchmark under the MXFP4 microscaling format. The recipe combines established techniques from Abecassis, Felix et al. [arXiv:2509.25149] (hybrid 1D/2D block quantization, randomized Hadamard transforms, and stochastic rounding) with a simplified weight de-oscillation scheme adapted from TetraJet-v2 [arXiv:2510.27527]. On C4 validation at global batch size 16, MXFP4 + RHT + SR + de-oscillation reaches a validation loss of 3.3350 at 16,128 steps, only 0.007 above the BF16 baseline (3.3283), closing roughly 50% of the gap left by MXFP4 without de-oscillation (3.3418). Measured by steps to reach the MLPerf quality target (validation loss 3.34), de-oscillation cuts the FP4 convergence overhead relative to BF16 from +20.0% to +5.0%. We also report negative end-to-end results from differential gradient estimation, outlier clipping, and macro-block scaling, despite each showing operator-level SNR gains. All experiments use simulated MXFP4 kernels on AMD MI300 hardware and wall-clock speed has not been optimized.

report.summary: An open-source ALTO recipe trains a 20B-parameter MoE model in MXFP4 with only 5% convergence overhead versus BF16, halving the FP4 quality gap using de-oscillation plus stochastic rounding.
report.background: Sub-8-bit training has become the next frontier for LLM economics: weight and activation memory traffic, not raw FLOPs, often limits throughput, and FP4 formats promise roughly 4x compression over BF16. Hardware has moved first — NVIDIA's Blackwell and AMD's MI300/MI355 generation ship native FP4 and MX (microscaling) block formats, and vLLM/SGLang already serve FP4 weights. But the OCP microscaling spec allows only a shared exponent per block (32 elements in MXFP4), so a single outlier can swamp a block and inject gradient noise that destabilizes momentum-based optimizers. Prior work showed FP4 training is possible but pays a convergence penalty; practitioners have therefore kept BF16 for pretraining and reserved FP4 for inference. MLPerf's Small MoE Training benchmark gave the community a fixed, reproducible target to measure that penalty.
key_points: ALTO stacks three known tricks — hybrid 1D/2D block quantization, randomized Hadamard transforms (which smear outliers across a block before rounding), and stochastic rounding — with a simplified weight de-oscillation scheme borrowed from TetraJet-v2 that damps quantization-driven weight jitter.

On C4 validation at global batch size 16, the full recipe reaches loss 3.3350 at 16,128 steps versus a BF16 baseline of 3.3283 — a 0.007 gap, roughly half the 0.0135 gap MXFP4 shows without de-oscillation.
Measured the way MLPerf actually scores, de-oscillation drops the extra steps needed to hit the 3.34 quality target from +20.0% over BF16 to +5.0%, the headline efficiency number.

Three plausible fixes failed end-to-end despite improving per-operator signal-to-noise ratio: differential gradient estimation, outlier clipping, and macro-block scaling — a useful warning that local SNR gains do not compose into faster convergence.
All results use simulated MXFP4 kernels on AMD MI300 with no wall-clock optimization, so the memory-bandwidth and throughput wins the format promises remain unmeasured.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the result reframes FP4 as a pretraining format rather than an inference-only convenience: a 5% step overhead is small enough that 4x smaller weight traffic could still net a large throughput win once kernels are real. That strengthens the case for Blackwell, MI300-class and successor hardware, and pressures MLPerf to keep an FP4 division honest. For developers, the recipe is open and built from published components, so small teams can experiment without inventing quantization schemes — but the simulated-kernel caveat means nobody should budget savings yet. For regular users, the near-term effect is indirect: cheaper training and serving of MoE models, more capable open-weight releases, and eventually lower API prices, with no visible change in product behavior.
report.tools: Start with GPT-OSS-20B, the open-weight MoE used here, and the ALTO recipe's components: arXiv:2509.25149 for block quantization, Hadamard transforms and stochastic rounding, and TetraJet-v2 (arXiv:2510.27527) for de-oscillation. For hands-on FP4, try torchao's MX and NVFP4 quantization paths plus the OCP Microscaling spec, and run the MLPerf Small MoE Training benchmark for comparable numbers. AMD's ROCm/MI300 stack is the reported hardware baseline.
